body.text: If 2024 was the year the world reckoned with a fraying multilateral order, 2025 put the global order further to the test. Tariffs as high as 50 percent complicated the dynamics of decades-old trade relationships; the momentum of artificial intelligence (AI) transformed into a race for data, compute, and standards; and resolutions to conflicts across multiple theatres remained elusive even as new fault lines emerged in the areas of climate, technology governance, and domestic politics. As we write this, the global order is not simply under strain; it is being actively reconstituted. India, like the rest of the Global South, must navigate a landscape where old assumptions about power, partnership, and predictability no longer hold.

The world is changing faster than our collective ability to fathom it and formulate a response. For India, navigating this new world demands a comprehensive national resilience spanning the military, economic, intellectual, and institutional domains, to be able to respond not just promptly but effectively.

It is against this backdrop that Observer Research Foundation, in partnership with Nalanda University, convened the 8th India Think Tank Forum on 12-13 January 2026, with the theme “India in the Changing World: Building Inner Resilience”. The Forum offered an opportunity to bring together voices across regions, disciplines, and generations, convened aptly at Nalanda University in Rajgir, Bihar, once among the world's greatest centres of learning and intellectual exchange. The site served as an appropriate backdrop for reflecting on how India rebuilds its own tradition of rigorous, collaborative enquiry.

This compendium builds on the insights shared at the Forum and aims to a) bridge the regional and linguistic divide by bringing together the voices of India's growing think tank community, and b) provide a coherent curation of ideas that matter to India's growth and foreign policy. The compendium carries thematically diverse essays inspired by the panel discussions during the Forum. We invited authors from across the Forum's nine sessions to reflect on the trends shaping their fields and the issues that emerged during the discussions in which they participated. The essays carry perspectives from think tank leaders, scholars, former practitioners, and analysts who engage with questions related to India's foreign policy and its evolving place in a fragmenting international order in their fields.

It is our hope that this collection of essays captures the essence of the Forum, at the heart of which lay a set of tough questions the Indian think tank community was asked to confront collectively: Are our analytical frameworks fit for a transactional, multipolar, tech-driven, and climate-affected world, or are we still operating through traditional assumptions of power and policy? Are we cultivating the intellectual depth and networks needed to decode these complexities and act on them collaboratively? How can India foster the intellectual and institutional resilience needed not merely to interpret a rapidly changing world but to read it correctly, act on it with foresight, and help shape its direction without losing coherence amidst global turbulence?

The Forum opened with the Inaugural Session, “The State of the World: Mapping Power, Disorder, and Direction”, which took stock of the inflection points of 2025 that cannot be ignored. The panel discussions focused on the redistribution of power; the weaponisation of technology and trade; and the reordering driven by climate action, demographic shifts, and digital transformation. They probed which of these shifts are structural and which are merely cyclical, and how middle powers and emerging economies can exert agency amidst great-power flux. Perhaps most critically, the discussion asked whether there is any coherence left in today's global landscape, and what India and the world should expect as the next decade unfolds.

The first thematic panel, “The AI Racecourse: Building India's Edge in an Age of Algorithmic Power”, examined India's position in a contest increasingly defined by data, compute, and regulatory influence concentrated in the hands of a few economies and corporations. Speakers considered which segments of the AI value chain India should prioritise to gain strategic advantage, how the country can build the talent pipelines and institutional capacity this requires, and what industrial and regulatory choices will allow India to move from being a “data mine” for global firms to a decisive player shaping global AI norms in its own right.

The panel “The Governance Gap: Internal and External Perspectives” turned the lens inward, examining how India's governance institutions are adapting to rising development demands amidst fiscal pressures and uneven state capacity. The discussion placed India in comparative perspective with other federal and developing countries, asking what lessons can be drawn from, and offered to them on decentralisation, welfare delivery, and state-led growth. Panellists explored whether India can craft a development-oriented governance model that reconciles national priorities with regional diversity, and what institutional reforms are needed to align state capacity with long-term development goals.

Building on the earlier themes, the panel “The Human-Machine Equation: Decoding AI's Impact on Indian Society” examined how AI is being woven into the core of India's governance, economy, and society—from defence and healthcare to welfare delivery. Speakers cautioned that AI systems built on narrow linguistic and cultural contexts risk amplifying structural inequalities as they enter critical sectors, and that AI-driven misinformation poses a growing threat to democratic trust. The discussion also explored whether India's current policies are equipped to address risks from generative AI, misuse of biometrics, and algorithmic bias, particularly given the country's continued dependence on foreign-built models.

Few challenges are as consequential for India as the energy transition, and the panel “The Next Energy Frontier: Scaling India's Transition for a Net-Zero Future” tackled the question of how India moves towards delivering system-wide transformation, having already met key Paris Agreement commitments ahead of schedule. India's challenge, speakers noted, today lies in execution: it must bridge the gap between installed capacity and actual generation, and design financing instruments and regulatory frameworks that make clean energy both reliable and affordable. The discussion also considered how India can leverage international finance, technology transfer, and climate diplomacy to champion the next phase of the global energy transition.

The panel “X + Y: Realising the Full Economic Potential of Indian Women” examined one of the more remarkable shifts in India's recent economic story: female labour force participation nearly doubling between 2017-18 and 2023-24. Speakers were candid, however, that this progress conceals a structural challenge: most women remain concentrated in informal, low-paying jobs that offer limited security or mobility. The discussion explored how policy, industry, and cultural change can together move women into formal, higher-productivity sectors. It also highlighted how India's economic narrative can move beyond tokenistic inclusion and position women’s participation as central to the country's productivity and competitiveness.

In the context of India’s accelerating defence modernisation, the panel "Future Force: Shaping India's 21st-Century Defence Posture" explored the twin challenge of technological self-reliance and adaptation to hybrid, multi-domain warfare. Despite the push for indigenisation under Atmanirbhar Bharat, speakers noted that critical dependencies persist as the nature of warfare shifts towards AI-enabled command systems, autonomous platforms, and cyber and information operations. The discussion examined how India can deepen defence partnerships through minilateral and bilateral arrangements without compromising strategic autonomy, and what a future-ready Indian defence ecosystem should look like by 2030.

The panel "Trade Wars and Tightropes: What Must India Do?" confronted the toughest stress test of India's export engine in years: the US decision to impose 50 percent tariffs on key Indian exports. Speakers assessed the real depth of the tariffs' impact on India's competitiveness and the structural shifts needed to build trade resilience. The discussion also explored how India can simultaneously negotiate with Washington and strengthen alternative trade and investment corridors with BRICS, ASEAN, and the wider Global South. With international trade increasingly being wielded as an instrument of foreign policy, the discussion asked what balance India should strike between economic pragmatism and geopolitical signalling.

Turning inward to the think tank community, the panel "Ideas & Ideals: Balancing Creativity, Competition, and Collaboration" reflected on the tension organisations in the policy ecosystem face between the stability they are built for and the adaptability the moment demands. Speakers considered how institutions can be designed as evolving systems capable of self-correction without losing their core mission, what governance and incentive structures can turn organisations into genuine "idea labs", and where the "collective gains" lie that might draw India's think tank community towards collaboration rather than competition.

The Forum closed with a session on the "2026 Roadmap for India", which drew together the key takeaways from the two days of discussions. It considered the role the think tank community must play in building the country's resilience in the year ahead.

The India Think Tank Forum 2026 proved useful not just for discussing the pressing ideas of our time but for assessing, individually and collectively, whether India's analytical frameworks and think tank ecosystem are able to keep pace with the complexities of the decade ahead. India's greatest strength, as the discussions repeatedly affirmed, cannot lie in size and scale alone, but in the clarity and conviction that come only from open, candid dialogue. As we continue to build this compendium into an annual publication, it is our hope that this volume offers a valuable direction for India's search for clarity, conviction, and resilience in an increasingly contested world.
